The table shows that the effect of low level development on the increased demand for services is likely to be very small, amounting to less than one percent in Lodge Grass and Crow Agency, and 1.5 percent in Wyola.
For the city of Hardin, the situation is more complex. The projected population in Hardin does not rise at a steady rate; thus, demands for services will also be irregular. Table III-7 shows the trends in facility needs for Hardin. The table includes the present capacities and the total demand in 1978, 1982, 1986, 1989 and 2000 for each facility. These years illustrate the extremes and the abrupt changes in demand for services associated with the LFPR-2 and AF-2 combination of assumptions. The change in demand during the intervening years is steady and moderate and is not shown here.
Except for solid waste disposal services, all municipal services in Hardin are operating at or near capacity. All facilities will require at least some expansion during the 25 year study period. As shown in Table III-7, the police, fire, and solid waste disposal requirements will be little affected by expected population fluctuations.
The services experiencing major impacts from population growth are the water and sewer systems, since these must be expanded with the addition of each new home. If low level (Scenario 1) development occurs, the water system must have an increase in capacity of over 200 percent by the year 2000, and the sewer system must have an expansion of nearly 100 percent during the same period.
